what: Merit Medical makes single-use devices used in minimally invasive procedures. Its products are the catheters, guidewires, inflation devices, drainage systems and embolisation materials that doctors use to work inside blood vessels and organs through small incisions rather than open surgery.
customers: Interventional cardiologists, radiologists, oncologists and the hospitals that stock their procedure rooms, across a very wide range of product lines.
money: Catheters, guidewires, inflation devices, embolisation and access products.
Devices for gastrointestinal and pulmonary procedures.
moat: Merit sells thousands of small, inexpensive, single-use items that doctors choose by familiarity and feel, and which get consumed with every procedure. That breadth is the moat: a hospital would rather buy a long list of items from one supplier it trusts than manage dozens of vendors, and a physician who likes a particular guidewire does not switch to save a few dollars.
risks: The shares trade at about 31.6 times earnings, 15.7 times EV/EBITDA and 24.8 times free cash flow, which is a full price.
Last year’s net margin was 8.5%, modest for a medical device company, because a very wide product range is expensive to manufacture and sell.
Growth is steady but unspectacular, from $1.1B in 2021 to $1.5B in 2025.
Debt of $821.6M against $446.4M of cash is manageable but has grown through acquisitions.
Twelve analysts average a $107.00 target, about 27% above the current price.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $1.1B in 2021 to $1.5B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $1.6B.
Free cash flow of $203.6M on $1.6B of revenue shows the business converts well.
Single-use devices are consumed with every procedure, which ties revenue to procedure volumes rather than equipment cycles.
Physicians choose these items by familiarity and feel, which makes substitution unusually unlikely for small-ticket products.
Minimally invasive procedures continue to replace open surgery, which grows the whole category.
watch: Procedure-driven revenue growth and gross margin. The breadth of the product line is the strength; whether it earns a better margin over time is the question.
view: Merit Medical sells the unglamorous consumables of modern medicine: the guidewire, the catheter, the inflation device, the drainage set. Each item is cheap, each is used once and thrown away, and a hospital buys thousands of them. The business model is excellent in one specific respect — revenue follows procedure volumes rather than hospital capital budgets, so it does not swing with equipment purchasing cycles.

The moat is breadth and physician habit, and both are more durable than they sound. A hospital procurement department would far rather buy a long list of items from one supplier it trusts than manage relationships with dozens. And an interventional cardiologist who likes the feel of a particular guidewire will not switch to save a few dollars on a product that costs less than the gloves — the clinical consequence of an unfamiliar device in a delicate procedure is not worth the saving.

The cost of that breadth shows in the margin. An 8.5% net margin is modest for medical devices, because manufacturing and selling thousands of distinct low-priced items is expensive: many production lines, many regulatory registrations, a large sales force calling on many specialties. Companies with one or two high-value products earn far more per dollar of revenue. The trade-off is that Merit’s revenue is far more diversified and far less exposed to any single product failing.

At 31.6 times earnings and 24.8 times free cash flow for a business growing revenue from $1.1 billion to $1.5 billion over four years, you are paying a quality multiple for steady mid-single-digit growth. That is defensible given the stickiness, and it is not cheap. The thing I would watch is gross margin: management has talked for years about improving it through manufacturing consolidation, and whether that happens determines whether this is a compounder or a reliable but ordinary business.
bull: Minimally invasive procedure volumes keep growing while physician habit and product breadth hold the position, and margin improvement programmes finally deliver.
bear: A 31 times earnings multiple meets mid-single-digit growth and a structurally modest 8.5% margin that manufacturing consolidation never improves.
